# IconButton

Figma: [02b. IconButton](https://www.figma.com/design/a7Z956YZy9n6f9uz5DK16Y?node-id=69-890) · Family: 02 Actions · Status: stable · Version 2.0.0 · Updated 2026-05-19

IconButton is a square action component for moments when a label would be redundant or take up too much room. Think close-X in a modal, copy-to-clipboard on a deal card, dismiss on a toast, or the back arrow in an app bar. It shares all 6 variants, 3 sizes, and 6 states with Button - but instead of a label, it carries a single centered icon that can be swapped per usage from the Syntropy Icons library.

Reference image (every variant, labelled): `knowledge/examples/components/icon-button/reference.png`

### IconButton

A square, label-less button carrying one centered icon, with the same six variants and states as Button. Used for compact, unambiguous actions such as closing a sheet, copying an IBAN or opening a more menu.

Level: organism

Use when:
- Close X on a BottomSheet, Modal or Toast: Variant=text
- Copy, share or bookmark actions on a deal card or list row: Variant=tertiary
- Retry next to a failed upload or network error: Variant=error with a refresh icon
- A trash icon to delete a draft or remove a document, followed by confirmation: Variant=destructive

Don't use when:
- The icon meaning is not universal (filter, sort, Sukuk, Sharia, KYC concepts): use Button with a leading icon and a label
- A back arrow in the app header: use BackButton
- The single main floating action of a screen: use FAB / Standard
- Navigating to another page with text: use Link

Accessibility: Every instance needs a verb-object semantic label (for example «نسخ رقم الآيبان»), and md/sm need parent padding to reach a 44pt tap target.

| Property in Figma | Code name | Type | Values | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Icon | `icon` | instance swap | default Button Icon Placeholder | 398:2 |
| Variant | `variant` | variant | primary, secondary, tertiary, destructive, error, text | primary |
| Size | `size` | variant | lg, md, sm | lg |
| State | `state` | variant | default, hover, pressed, focused, disabled, loading | default |

## Guide from the doc page

### Overview

An IconButton is a Button without a label - a single centered icon inside a square tap target. Use it when the icon's meaning is unambiguous on its own (close ✕, copy 📋, share ↗) or when label-and-icon would crowd a dense layout (toolbar buttons, list row actions, card-corner controls).

IconButton uses the same 6 variants, 3 sizes, and 6 states as Button - so the semantic intent of each color is identical. A primary IconButton is still "the main action," a destructive IconButton is still "this will damage something," and so on. The only thing that changes is the chrome: square instead of pill-shaped, icon instead of label.

### Live preview - one of each variant

### Anatomy

An IconButton is a square frame with a single icon centered inside. There is no leading or trailing slot - just one icon, one swap property. The square dimensions match the size scale: 32×32 at sm, 40×40 at md, 48×48 at lg. The icon inside is proportionally smaller so it visually centers without crowding the tap target.

**1. Container**
Square frame at 32/40/48px (sm/md/lg). Fills, strokes, and corner radius bind to the same semantic tokens as Button. The container IS the tap target - no extra padding needed.

**2. Icon**
Single centered 16/20/24px icon (sm/md/lg). Swappable via Icon instance-swap property - defaults to placeholder, overridden in product to a real icon from the Syntropy Icons library. Icon color follows the variant's text/icon token.

### Variants

Six variants - same intent as Button. Variant tells the user what KIND of action this is (main? destructive? quiet?). Without a label to clarify intent, the variant's color does even more work in IconButton than in Button - pick deliberately.

| Primary Solid green fill, white icon. Highest emphasis. Reserved for the single most important action the user can take without a label - usually because the icon is universally understood (e.g. forward arrow on a wizard). | When to use A floating action on a key surface where one tap moves the user forward. Rare for IconButton - most icon-only actions don't deserve primary loudness. |
| --- | --- |

| Secondary Outlined with green border, green icon. Visually quieter than primary, still clearly actionable. | When to use Inline toolbar actions next to a primary CTA. Camera capture next to "Submit photo." The outline reads as "available, but not the main action." |
| --- | --- |

| Tertiary Subtle green-tinted background with default (dark) icon. Visually quiet. Same WCAG advantage as Button tertiary - passes AAA easily. | When to use Embedded actions in cards or list rows - bookmark, share, more options. Available when reached for but doesn't pull attention away from the card's content. |
| --- | --- |

| Destructive Solid red fill, white icon. Reserved for icon-only actions that delete, remove, or irreversibly change state. The red on its own is the signal - pair with confirmation if the action is non-undoable. | When to use A trash icon to delete a draft. An X to permanently dismiss a high-stakes item. Anything where the user clicking by mistake would lose data they care about. |
| --- | --- |

| Error Subtle red fill, red icon, red border. Signals "this action is blocked or related to an error state" without being destructive itself. | When to use A retry icon on a failed upload. A refresh icon next to a network-error indicator. Communicates problem-state without implying the click itself is dangerous. |
| --- | --- |

| Text (ghost) No fill, no border, green icon. The lowest-affordance IconButton - visually indistinguishable from a free-floating icon until hovered. Hover state adds a subtle background to confirm clickability. | When to use Close X in modals and toasts. Dismiss icons. Back arrows in app bars where the surrounding chrome carries the affordance. Anywhere the visual context tells the user "this is clickable" so the button doesn't need to. |
| --- | --- |

### Sizes

Three square sizes match the Button height scale. Critical: 32×32 sm falls below Apple's 44pt touch target minimum - use sm only in mouse-driven web contexts or surround it with parent padding that brings the effective touch target to 44+pt.

Large (lg)

| Container size | 48×48px |
| --- | --- |
| Icon size | 24px |
| Visual padding | 12px each side |
| Meets 44pt tap target | Yes |
Medium (md) · default

| Container size | 40×40px |
| --- | --- |
| Icon size | 20px |
| Visual padding | 10px each side |
| Meets 44pt tap target | No - add padding around |
Small (sm)

| Container size | 32×32px |
| --- | --- |
| Icon size | 16px |
| Visual padding | 8px each side |
| Meets 44pt tap target | No - add padding around |

### States

Same six states as Button: default, hover, pressed, focused, disabled, loading. In Flutter, gesture detection collapses default → hover → pressed automatically. The loading state replaces the icon with three dots to communicate async work without needing a separate spinner component.

Default

Resting state. No user interaction.

Hover

Cursor is over the button (desktop/web). Background shifts to primary-hover. Not rendered on Flutter mobile.

Pressed

Button is being actively clicked/tapped. Background shifts to primary-pressed.

Focused

2px focus ring (border/focus → text/default) wraps the button - visible against any background.

Disabled

Cannot be activated. Background and icon shift to disabled tokens. Pointer events blocked at runtime.

Loading

Async action in progress. Icon is replaced by three dots. Pointer events blocked.

### Direction handling - RTL

Unlike Button, IconButton does NOT ship with a Direction variant axis. The icon sits centered inside a square - its visual position does not change between LTR and RTL. The semantic meaning of the icon, however, often DOES change with direction.

Some icons are directional: chevron-right ("forward" in LTR) becomes chevron-left ("forward" in RTL). Some are not: settings-gear, plus, more-dots, search - these mean the same thing regardless of direction.

How to handle direction correctly: at the call site, swap the IconButton's Icon property to the right-pointing variant in LTR and to the left-pointing variant in RTL. The Syntropy Icons library provides mirrored pairs for every directional icon - they share a base name with a "-rtl" suffix or come from a single chevron component with a Direction variant.

> **Info:** There is no SafqahIconButtonRTL widget in the Flutter implementation. Code consumes one SafqahIconButton; the icon parameter is what changes with direction. In Flutter, you can detect direction via Directionality.of(context).

> **Warning:** Do NOT auto-mirror IconButton's container via Transform.scale(scaleX: -1). That would also flip text-bearing icons (search magnifier, etc.) which look broken when mirrored. Always pick the correct icon at the call site instead of flipping geometrically.

### Icons

The single most important thing about IconButton is that the icon does ALL the communication. There's no label to clarify what the action is. Pick icons whose meaning is universally understood, and pair with a tooltip or aria-label for anything ambiguous.

Icon sizes match Button - 16/20/24px for sm/md/lg. Always pull icons from the Syntropy Icons library so they're properly themed for light and dark mode, optically aligned, and consistent in stroke weight. Custom pasted SVGs will look wrong somewhere.

> **Warning:** If the icon is not universally understood (e.g. "kebab menu" is OK but "compass-rose" rarely is), you must add a tooltip showing the action label on hover, AND a semanticLabel/aria-label for screen readers. An IconButton with an ambiguous icon and no label is invisible to assistive tech and confusing to mouse users.

> **Tip:** Common icon-only patterns that work without tooltips: close (✕), more (⋯), back (←), search (🔍), settings (⚙), bookmark, share, copy, delete (🗑), edit (✎). Common patterns that DO need tooltips: filter icons, sort icons, anything domain-specific (Sukuk, Sharia, KYC). When in doubt, add the tooltip.

### Code examples

How engineering consumes IconButton. Note the required semanticLabel parameter on every example - this is non-optional.

### Flutter / Dart

```dart
SafqahIconButton(
  icon: SafqahIcons.close,
  variant: SafqahIconButtonVariant.text,
  size: SafqahIconButtonSize.md,
  semanticLabel: 'Close dialog',
  onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context),
)

// Destructive with confirmation
SafqahIconButton(
  icon: SafqahIcons.trash,
  variant: SafqahIconButtonVariant.destructive,
  size: SafqahIconButtonSize.md,
  semanticLabel: 'Delete draft',
  onPressed: () => _confirmAndDelete(),
)

// Loading state
SafqahIconButton(
  icon: SafqahIcons.refresh,
  variant: SafqahIconButtonVariant.tertiary,
  size: SafqahIconButtonSize.sm,
  semanticLabel: 'Refresh portfolio',
  isLoading: _refreshing,
  onPressed: _refreshing ? null : _refresh,
)

// RTL: pick the right icon at the call site
final isRtl = Directionality.of(context) == TextDirection.rtl;
SafqahIconButton(
  icon: isRtl ? SafqahIcons.chevronLeft : SafqahIcons.chevronRight,
  variant: SafqahIconButtonVariant.text,
  semanticLabel: 'Next step',
  onPressed: _nextStep,
)
```

### React / TypeScript (web prototype)

```typescript
<IconButton
  icon={<CloseIcon />}
  variant="text"
  size="md"
  aria-label="Close dialog"
  onClick={onClose}
/>

// With tooltip for non-obvious icons
<Tooltip content="Filter by status">
  <IconButton
    icon={<FilterIcon />}
    variant="tertiary"
    size="sm"
    aria-label="Filter by status"
    onClick={openFilterMenu}
  />
</Tooltip>
```

### Usage - Do and Don't

Concrete IconButton scenarios from real Safqah surfaces. Pay attention to which variant is used, what icon is chosen, and how the surrounding context provides (or fails to provide) the affordance.

- **Do** · Scenario · Modal close button: Text variant for the close X. The modal's own chrome makes it obvious the X is clickable - the IconButton stays quiet so the modal content keeps focus.
- **Don't** · Scenario · Modal close button: Destructive (red) on the close X reads as "this will damage your data." Closing a modal is not destructive - it's navigational. Wrong tone entirely.
- **Do** · Scenario · Delete draft from a deal card: Destructive variant + trash icon. The red gives the user the visual pause they need before deleting a draft they spent time on. Pair with a confirmation dialog.
- **Don't** · Scenario · Delete draft from a deal card: Text variant on a delete trash icon is too quiet. Users may click thinking it's a less consequential action. Destructive must look destructive.
- **Do** · Scenario · Toolbar with multiple actions: All toolbar actions tertiary at the same size. Visually grouped, all equally available, none competing for primary attention. The toolbar itself carries the affordance.
- **Don't** · Scenario · Toolbar with multiple actions: Mixed variants in a toolbar implies hierarchy that doesn't exist. Why is one action primary green when the others are tertiary? The user pauses to figure that out instead of acting.
- **Do** · Scenario · Refresh on a failed API call: Error variant + refresh icon. The red signals "something is wrong with this action right now" while still offering the user the retry path. Matches the error state of the surrounding UI.
- **Don't** · Scenario · Refresh on a failed API call: Primary green on a retry button next to an error message creates dissonance - the green says "everything's fine, click here" while the error message says the opposite. Use error variant.
- **Do** · Scenario · "More options" kebab menu: Text variant for the three-dots menu. The kebab is a universally understood "more" affordance - no chrome needed. Quiet, predictable, gets out of the way.
- **Don't** · Scenario · "More options" kebab menu: Outlined secondary on a kebab menu adds chrome that competes with the row content. The kebab's recognizability already carries the affordance - the outline is wasted ink.
- **Do** · Scenario · Direction-sensitive - wizard back/forward: Pick chevron-left for "back" in LTR (chevron-right in RTL). At the call site, swap to the mirrored Syntropy icon based on Directionality.of(context). The IconButton itself stays the same.
- **Don't** · Scenario · Direction-sensitive - wizard back/forward: Using the same chevron-right icon for "back" in both LTR and RTL. In RTL screens, "back" should point right (toward where the user came from). The icon is wrong, not the IconButton.

### Notes from the maintainer

Six things to internalize before reaching for IconButton in your designs or code.

> **Info:** When to use IconButton over Button: only when the icon's meaning is unambiguous AND the surface is dense enough that a label would clutter. If you're unsure whether users will understand the icon, just use Button with leading icon and a label. Better one extra word than a confused user.

> **Warning:** semanticLabel is non-negotiable. Every IconButton in production must pass a verb-object accessibility label. The Flutter widget asserts this at construction. There is no acceptable default - every usage is different.

> **Tip:** Choosing the right icon: use the Syntropy Icons library, never custom SVGs. The library handles 2-mode theming, stroke width consistency, optical centering, and (for directional icons) LTR/RTL pairs. Custom SVGs will look wrong in dark mode or break visual rhythm.

> **Info:** RTL is handled at the icon level, not the IconButton level. Pick chevron-right in LTR and chevron-left in RTL at the call site - the IconButton container itself is direction-agnostic. Do not flip geometrically with Transform.scale.

> **Warning:** Anti-patterns we keep seeing: (1) IconButton without semanticLabel - broken for assistive tech. (2) primary variant on a close X - overweighted dismiss. (3) destructive on a "Close" or "Cancel" - wrong tone, that's navigation. (4) sm size in a mobile touch context without parent padding - fails the 44pt target rule. (5) ambiguous icons with no tooltip - confusing.

> **Tip:** External resources to internalize: Material 3 icon button guidance, WAI-ARIA patterns for icon-only controls, and WCAG 2.5.5 for touch targets. Internal: Syntropy Icons library (for the actual icons) and Safqah Brand Guidelines (for tone of voice in tooltips and labels).
